analysis.one_liner: Mandates 100% renewable electricity by 2035, efficiency targets, and net-zero emissions by 2050.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on November 18, 2025 with zero cosponsors and has been referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the share of U.S. electricity generated from renewable sources to rise every year until all electricity sold at the retail level is renewable by 2035. It would set steadily rising energy-saving targets for electric and natural gas suppliers through 2032, which suppliers could meet through a trading system. It would also require the EPA to set annual greenhouse gas reduction targets so that U.S. emissions in 2035 are at least 52% below 2005 levels and reach zero by 2050.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people benefit through cleaner air, reduced climate-related damage from heat waves, wildfires, storms, and sea-level rise, and lower energy use that the bill's findings say can save consumers money. Renewable energy companies and related manufacturers would gain from a guaranteed growing market for their products.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households exposed to pollution and climate damage

how_it_helps.text: Requires 100% of retail electricity to come from renewable sources by 2035, phasing in annually beginning in 2026 [S3].

Sets cumulative electricity savings targets reaching 11.25% and natural gas savings targets reaching 4.05% for retail suppliers by 2032, achieved through efficiency improvements at customer facilities [S3].
Requires EPA to set annual emissions targets ensuring 2035 emissions are at least 52% below 2005 levels and 2050 emissions are zero, with final implementing regulations within seven years [S3].
Allows suppliers to meet efficiency targets through a market-based trading system rather than direct compliance [S3].
Explicitly preserves state authority to adopt stronger renewable energy and climate policies [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers and coal-reliant utilities would lose sales as renewable mandates phase in. Electric and gas suppliers would bear compliance costs, which could be passed to consumers through rates, though efficiency savings could offset some of that. Climate policy debates of this kind typically also raise objections about grid reliability and consumer energy prices.

drawbacks.text: A 100% renewable retail electricity requirement by 2035, roughly a decade after enactment, is an aggressive timeline that critics would argue could strain grid reliability and raise electricity costs during the transition [S3].

Compliance costs for retail electric and gas suppliers under the efficiency and emissions mandates could be passed through to consumers in rates, at least partially offsetting the savings from efficiency [S3].
The bill relies heavily on agency rulemaking, with EPA regulations due within seven years of enactment, leaving much of the real burden to future administrations to design and enforce [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver large long-term benefits for public health and climate protection, but it asks the energy sector to transform very quickly and there is a real risk of higher electricity costs or reliability problems if the renewable buildout falls behind the mandate. The efficiency trading system and the preservation of stronger state rules soften the design somewhat. As introduced, the measure is more of a statement of targets than a detailed implementation plan; most of the hard choices are left to federal agencies.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and has not advanced since.

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Lieu introduced the bill on November 18, 2025 [S1].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, its first and only action to date [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With no cosponsors and no committee action, fossil fuel interests and utilities facing the mandates are better off with the bill stalled; households have gained nothing because the bill's protections remain on paper only.

for.name: Rep. Ted Lieu
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Climate Solutions Act of 2025 on November 18, 2025

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no action on it since introduction

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Controls the House floor and committee scheduling
against.what_they_did: Bills with no cosponsors in a chamber controlled by the opposing party are not brought to the floor

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor is a Democrat and the bill has zero cosponsors from either party, and it sits in a committee led by the Republican majority.

industries.note: Renewable electricity mandates and net-zero emission targets would shrink demand for coal, oil, and natural gas over time. Their interest in the bill stalling runs against the public health and climate benefits the bill targets.

Utilities would face rising renewable purchase requirements and efficiency savings targets, raising compliance costs that could reach consumers through rates. Some utilities with large renewable portfolios could adapt more easily than coal-reliant ones.

A 100% renewable electricity mandate and cumulative efficiency targets guarantee a growing market for wind, solar, storage, and efficiency services. Their gain comes alongside the bill's public benefits.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action beyond referral, the bill is very unlikely to advance. Most single-sponsor climate bills in a chamber controlled by the opposing party die quietly in committee without a hearing or a vote.
